requirements: The core contributions of 'Discount Model Search for Quality Diversity Optimization in High-Dimensional Measure Spaces' have been reproduced, including the DMS algorithm, the QDDM setting with two new image-based domains, and the experiments demonstrating that DMS outperforms CMA-MAE and other black-box QD algorithms across benchmark and QDDM domains.

sub_tasks.requirements: The environment, pyribs-based infrastructure, and shared experimental configuration (10,000 iterations, archive configurations, common hyperparameters) for reproducing the experiments have been set up correctly.

The pyribs library has been installed and used as the implementation framework for DMS and all baseline algorithms, consistent with the paper's statement that 'We implement all algorithms with pyribs (Tjanaka et al., 2023)'.

The compute environment provides the GPU acceleration that the paper's implementation relies on, consistent with Appendix F's description of a workstation with a 64-core (128-thread) AMD Ryzen Threadripper, an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU, and 64GB of RAM.

The discount model of DMS is trained on the GPU in all domains, with the model requiring roughly 300-400MB of GPU memory, per Appendix F ('In all domains, we train the discount model of DMS on the GPU. The discount model typically requires 300-400MB of GPU memory').
Triangle rasterization in TA (MNIST) and TA (F-MNIST) is accelerated on the GPU, per Appendix F ('In TA (MNIST) and TA (F-MNIST), we accelerate rendering of the triangles on the GPU').
StyleGAN3 generation and CLIP scoring in LSI (Hiker) are accelerated on the GPU, per Appendix F ('In LSI (Hiker), we accelerate StyleGAN3 and CLIP with the GPU').

The 20 trials of each algorithm in the benchmark domains are run in parallel, while algorithms in the QDDM domains are run serially, per Appendix F ('In benchmark domains, we run all 20 trials of each algorithm in parallel. In QDDM domains, we run algorithms serially').
All algorithms (DMS, CMA-MAE, DDS, MAP-Elites (line), MAP-Elites) are run for 10,000 iterations in every domain, as stated in Appendix C ('All algorithms run for 10,000 iterations').

The number of solutions generated and evaluated per iteration is equal across all algorithms in a given domain: for DMS, CMA-MAE, and DDS this equals W (number of emitters) times λ (emitter batch size), while for MAP-Elites and MAP-Elites (line) this equals the batch size λ, matching the per-domain values in Table 6 (e.g., W=15, λ=36 for 2D/10D LP domains giving 540 total evaluations, matching MAP-Elites batch size of 540).

For DMS, the total number of solutions generated and evaluated per iteration equals W (number of emitters) times λ (emitter batch size), as specified in Appendix C ('this number is equivalent to the number of emitters W times the emitter batch size λ').

For MAP-Elites, the total number of solutions generated and evaluated per iteration equals the batch size λ alone (no separate emitter count), as stated in Appendix C ('In the two MAP-Elites algorithms, this number is equivalent to the batch size λ').

In every LP benchmark domain, DMS, CMA-MAE, and DDS are configured with W=15 emitters and emitter batch size lambda=36 (540 evaluations per iteration), equal to the lambda=540 batch size configured for MAP-Elites and MAP-Elites (line) in those domains, so that all five algorithms consume an identical evaluation budget per iteration, per Table 6 and Appendix C.

In LSI (Hiker), DMS and CMA-MAE are configured with W=1 emitter and emitter batch size lambda=36 (36 evaluations per iteration), equal to the lambda=36 batch size configured for MAP-Elites and MAP-Elites (line) in that domain, so that all four algorithms consume an identical evaluation budget per iteration, per Table 6.

In Arm Repertoire, DMS, CMA-MAE, and DDS are configured with W=15 emitters and emitter batch size lambda=36 (540 evaluations per iteration), equal to the lambda=540 batch size configured for MAP-Elites and MAP-Elites (line) in that domain, so that all five algorithms consume an identical evaluation budget per iteration, per Table 6.
In all domains, the objective function is normalized to be between 0 and 1, so that the minimum objective f_min is set to 0, as stated in Appendix C.
For benchmark domains with 10D measure spaces (10D LP (Sphere), 10D LP (Rastrigin), 10D LP (Flat)), the archive is configured as a 10,000-cell CVT archive, per Appendix C.

For benchmark domains with 2D measure spaces (2D LP (Sphere), 2D LP (Rastrigin), 2D LP (Flat), and Arm Repertoire), the archive is configured as a 10,000-cell grid arranged as 100x100, per Appendix C ('the archive has 10,000 cells, arranged as a 100 x 100 grid for domains with 2D measure spaces').

In all domains except LSI (Hiker), the discount model is a small MLP taking raw measures as input, constructed exactly as specified in Appendix C.

The discount model is a three-layer MLP with layer sizes [k, 128, 128, 1], where k is the dimensionality of the measure space (e.g. [2,128,128,1] for 2D LP, [784,128,128,1] for the TA domains), per Appendix C.

The discount model MLP applies a ReLU activation after every layer except the output layer, so the scalar discount value is produced by an unactivated linear output, per Appendix C ('There is ReLU activation after every layer except the output layer').

The discount model networks are instantiated with the default PyTorch initialization rather than a custom initialization scheme, per Appendix C ('Networks are instantiated with the default PyTorch initialization').

A neural network is used as the discount model rather than a kernel-based method such as a kernel density/regression estimator, following Section 5's stated design choice ('While alternative models like kernel-based methods (Chen, 2017) are feasible, we select neural networks because the inductive biases of their various architectures make them suitable for many types of measures') and Appendix C.1's justification.

In LSI (Hiker), the discount model architecture embeds measures (images) with the vision transformer of CLIP before passing them into a three-layer MLP with layer sizes [512, 128, 128, 1], per Appendix C.

Inputs to the discount model network are normalized to the range [-1, 1] using the bounds of the measure space for that domain (e.g. [-256, 256] per dimension for 2D LP), per Appendix C ('Inputs to the network are normalized to the range [-1, 1] based on the bounds of the measure space').

For domains whose measures are images, the measure-space bounds used for the [-1, 1] input normalization are assumed to be [0, 1] per pixel, per Appendix C ('in the case of images, these bounds are assumed to be [0, 1]').
The discount model training procedure is implemented exactly as specified in Appendix C, covering the optimizer, loss, batching, and per-iteration stopping criterion.

The discount model is trained with an Adam optimizer using a learning rate of 0.001, per Appendix C ('The discount models are trained with an Adam optimizer with settings of learning rate alpha = 0.001'). Note this optimizer learning rate is distinct from the archive learning rate alpha of Eq. 1, despite the paper reusing the symbol alpha for both.
The Adam optimizer used to train the discount model is configured with beta1 = 0.9 and beta2 = 0.999, per Appendix C.

The discount model regression uses mean squared error (MSE) as the loss function between the model's predicted discount value and the target t_A, per Appendix C ('The loss function is mean squared error (MSE)').
The discount model is trained with a minibatch size of 32 over the dataset D_A, per Appendix C ('we train with a batch size of 32').

On each iteration the discount model is trained until the average loss over the whole dataset D_A falls to at most a cutoff of 0.05, per Appendix C ('the model trains until an average cutoff loss of at most 0.05 is reached over the whole dataset D_A').

Discount model training on each iteration is capped at a maximum of five epochs, so that training terminates even when the 0.05 average-loss cutoff is not reached, per Appendix C ('with a maximum of five epochs allowed').

The same loss-cutoff-and-epoch-cap training procedure is also applied during the initial pre-training of the discount model to output f_min at the n_init sampled cell centers (Algorithm 1 line 3), per Appendix C ('Each iteration (including during the initial training of the model to output f_min)').

A single Adam optimizer instance is maintained across the entire run, so that optimizer state (moment estimates, step count) persists between iterations rather than being reinitialized each time the discount model is retrained, per Appendix C ('The optimizer is maintained throughout the entire run').

The reproduced runs show that discount model training almost always requires only a single epoch to reach the 0.05 average cutoff loss, consistent with Appendix C ('In practice, we found that training almost always required only one epoch to reach a cutoff loss of 0.05').

Nearest-neighbour search for CVT archive cell assignment is performed with a k-D tree (Bentley, 1975) in the benchmark domains and the TA domains, per Appendix C.2 ('we were able to use k-D trees for all the benchmark domains and the TA domains').

For measure spaces of 10 dimensions or more, the k-D tree query is parallelized across 8 workers to improve efficiency, per Appendix C.2 ('for higher dimensions (10D or more), we further improved efficiency by allowing the k-D tree to use multiple workers (8 workers, specifically)').

Cell assignment in the TA domains remains tractable despite the 784-dimensional measure space because the archive contains only 1000 centroids, so brute-force-equivalent nearest-neighbour performance is acceptable, per Appendix C.2 ('although the TA domains had a 784-dimensional measure space, the archives only had 1000 centroids, making brute force performance acceptable').

For LSI (Hiker), nearest neighbor search precomputes CLIP embeddings for all 10,000 archive centroids and performs search over these 512-dimensional embeddings using scikit-learn's NearestNeighbors implementation, per Appendix C.2.

The Discount Model Search (DMS) algorithm has been implemented correctly, including the archive, CMA-ES emitters, the neural network discount model, the threshold-update target rule (Eq. 1), and the empty points mechanism, following Algorithm 1.

DMS maintains a MAP-Elites-style archive that retains the best solution found in each cell, but unlike CMA-MAE, DMS does not store discount or threshold values in the archive cells themselves, per Section 5 ('DMS maintains a MAP-Elites-style archive that retains the best solutions found... Unlike CMA-MAE, DMS does not store discount or threshold values in the archive').

At the start of a run DMS initializes an empty archive A together with the discount model f_hat_A(.; psi) and its parameters psi, before any pre-training or emitter setup, matching line 2 of Algorithm 1 ('Initialize empty archive A; discount model f_hat_A(.; psi) with parameters psi').

DMS initializes all W emitters with mean theta* set to the supplied initial solution theta_0, covariance Sigma set to sigma*I where sigma is the domain's initial step size, and fresh internal CMA-ES parameters p, matching line 4 of Algorithm 1 ('Initialize W emitters, each with mean theta* <- theta_0, covariance Sigma <- sigma*I, internal parameters p').

A complete DMS run generates and evaluates exactly N*W*lambda solutions, storing elites in the archive A, matching the Result clause of Algorithm 1 ('Generates NW lambda solutions, storing elites in an archive A').

DMS maintains W CMA-ES-based emitters that sample solutions from a Gaussian distribution N(theta*, Sigma) and update their distribution parameters based on archive improvement rankings computed via the discount model, matching lines 3-9 and 18 of Algorithm 1.

Each DMS emitter restarts with mean theta* set to a random solution from the archive, covariance Sigma reset to sigma*I, and new internal CMA-ES parameters p, when CMA-ES converges (per the domain's configured restart rule), matching lines 19-20 of Algorithm 1.

For each sampled solution theta_i, DMS computes the archive improvement Delta_i = f(theta_i) - f_hat_A(m(theta_i)) using the discount model's current output rather than a histogram value, matching line 11 of Algorithm 1.

When a new solution theta_i is evaluated, DMS computes its archive cell e via calculate_archive_cell and replaces the current elite theta_e in that cell only if f(theta_i) > f(theta_e), matching lines 14-16 of Algorithm 1 (standard MAP-Elites replacement rule).

The discount model is implemented as a neural network f_hat_A(.; psi) parameterized by psi that takes measures as input and outputs a scalar discount value, approximating the true discount function f_A: R^k -> R, per Section 5's description of the Discount Model component.

Before the main loop, DMS samples n_init cells from the (initially empty) archive and regresses the discount model to output the minimum objective f_min at the centers of these cells, reflecting that the archive starts empty, matching line 3 of Algorithm 1.

For each emitter-sampled solution theta, DMS creates a dataset entry (s, t_A) with s = m(theta) (the solution's measures) and t_A computed via the threshold-update target rule, appending it to the dataset D_A, matching lines 12-13 of Algorithm 1.

The target t_A for each emitter-sampled solution is computed via Eq. 1: t_A = f_hat_A(s) if f(theta) <= f_hat_A(s), otherwise t_A = (1 - alpha) * f_hat_A(s) + alpha * f(theta), where alpha is the archive learning rate, reproducing CMA-MAE's threshold update rule in continuous form.

When the objective value f(theta) of the emitter-sampled solution is less than or equal to the discount model's current output f_hat_A(s) at that solution's measures s, the target t_A is set exactly equal to f_hat_A(s), i.e., the discount model output is left unchanged for that entry, matching the first branch of Eq. 1.

When the objective value f(theta) of the emitter-sampled solution exceeds the discount model's current output f_hat_A(s), the target t_A is computed as the linear combination (1 - alpha) * f_hat_A(s) + alpha * f(theta), matching the second branch of Eq. 1.

The archive learning rate alpha used in Eq. 1's target computation is the same per-domain alpha hyperparameter configured for DMS in Table 6 (e.g., alpha=0.1 for 2D LP (Sphere), alpha=1.0 for LSI (Hiker)), controlling how quickly the discount model's targets shift toward the objective value of newly discovered solutions.

The f_hat_A(s) term used in both branches of Eq. 1 refers to the discount model's current (most recently trained) output at measures s = m(theta), not a stored histogram cell value, correctly implementing the shift from CMA-MAE's discrete threshold t_e to DMS's continuous discount model output.

The Eq. 1 target rule is verified to be the continuous analogue of CMA-MAE's discrete threshold update t_e <- (1-alpha)*t_e + alpha*f(theta') for solutions that improve the cell, and to leave the threshold unchanged for solutions that do not improve the cell, exactly as described in Section 5's explanation directly following Eq. 1.

On each iteration, DMS samples n_empty unoccupied cells (without replacement) from the archive, computes the centers of these cells, and extends the dataset D_A with entries (center, f_min) for each sampled empty cell, matching lines 21-23 of Algorithm 1.

If there are fewer than n_empty unoccupied archive cells available, DMS selects all such unoccupied cells rather than failing or sampling with replacement, per the clarification in Section 5 ('If there are fewer than n_empty unoccupied archive cells, we select all such cells').

For CVT archives used in DMS, the 'center' of a cell used for empty-point sampling and initial pre-training is defined as that cell's centroid, per the note in Section 5 ('in the CVT archive, the "center" of the cell is that cell's centroid').

At the end of each iteration, DMS regresses the discount model f_hat_A on the full collected dataset D_A (containing both emitter-sampled entries and empty-point entries), matching line 24 of Algorithm 1.

The DMS main loop correctly interleaves the two phases described in Section 5's Summary: (1) sampling solutions from emitters and ranking them by discount-model-based improvement to update CMA-ES distributions, and (2) collecting the dataset D_A and retraining the discount model f_hat_A, executed once per iteration for N iterations.

Within each of the N main-loop iterations of DMS, Phase 1 is executed first: all W emitters sample their batches of lambda solutions each from their current Gaussian distributions N(theta*, Sigma), evaluate objective and measures for each solution, compute improvement values Delta_i using the discount model's current output, rank the solutions within each emitter by Delta_i, and use this ranking to adapt each emitter's CMA-ES distribution parameters theta*, Sigma, and internal parameters p, matching lines 6-18 of Algorithm 1.
For each of the W emitters, lambda solutions theta_i are sampled from the emitter's current Gaussian distribution N(theta*, Sigma), matching line 9 of Algorithm 1 (theta_i ~ N(theta*, Sigma)).

For each sampled solution theta_i, the objective f(theta_i) and measures m(theta_i) are computed via the domain's eval function, matching line 10 of Algorithm 1 (f(theta_i), m(theta_i) <- eval(theta_i)).

For each sampled solution theta_i, the archive improvement value Delta_i is computed as f(theta_i) minus the discount model's current output f_hat_A(m(theta_i)), matching line 11 of Algorithm 1 (Delta_i <- f(theta_i) - f_hat_A(m(theta_i))), using the discount model's output rather than a stored histogram value.

For each sampled solution theta_i, the discount value target t_A,i is computed via Eq. 1 using s = m(theta_i), and the pair (m(theta_i), t_A,i) is appended to the dataset D_A, matching lines 12-13 of Algorithm 1.

For each sampled solution theta_i, the archive cell e is computed via calculate_archive_cell(A, m(theta_i)), matching line 14 of Algorithm 1, correctly locating the cell (or CVT centroid) corresponding to the solution's measures.

For each sampled solution theta_i, if f(theta_i) is greater than f(theta_e) (the objective of the solution currently in cell e), theta_e is replaced with theta_i in the archive, matching lines 15-16 of Algorithm 1, implementing the standard MAP-Elites greedy replacement rule.

Within each emitter, the batch of sampled solutions theta_i is ranked according to their improvement values Delta_i, matching line 17 of Algorithm 1 (Rank theta_i by Delta_i), producing the ranking used to drive the CMA-ES update.

Based on the improvement ranking Delta_i, each emitter's CMA-ES distribution mean theta*, covariance Sigma, and internal parameters p (e.g., evolution paths, step-size control parameters) are adapted, matching line 18 of Algorithm 1 (Adapt theta*, Sigma, p based on improvement ranking Delta_i), following standard CMA-ES update rules driven by the improvement-based ranking rather than raw objective values.

Phase 1's sampling, evaluation, improvement computation, archive updates, ranking, and CMA-ES adaptation are performed independently for each of the W emitters within the same iteration (i.e., the inner 'for Emitter 1..Emitter W' loop of Algorithm 1 lines 7-20 is executed for every emitter before proceeding to Phase 2), so that each emitter maintains and updates its own distribution parameters theta*, Sigma, and p without interference from other emitters' samples.

During Phase 1 of a given iteration, the discount model f_hat_A used to compute Delta_i and t_A,i for all emitters and all solutions remains fixed at its value from the end of the previous iteration's training (i.e., it is not updated mid-Phase-1), so that all emitters within the same iteration are ranked against a consistent discount function, consistent with the discount model retraining occurring only in Phase 2 (line 24) after all emitter sampling in Phase 1 (lines 7-20) has completed.

Within each of the N main-loop iterations of DMS, Phase 2 is executed after Phase 1 completes for all emitters: the dataset D_A (populated during Phase 1 with emitter-sampled entries, then extended with empty-point entries from unoccupied archive cells) is used to regress and update the discount model f_hat_A's parameters psi, matching lines 21-24 of Algorithm 1.

At the start of Phase 2 (after Phase 1 completes for all W emitters), n_empty unoccupied cells are sampled without replacement from the archive A (or all unoccupied cells if fewer than n_empty exist), matching line 21 of Algorithm 1 ('Sample n_empty unoccupied cells e_1..n_empty from archive A without replacement').

The centers s_1..n_empty of the sampled unoccupied cells are computed (using CVT centroids where applicable) and appended to the dataset D_A as entries (s, f_min) for each sampled empty cell, matching lines 22-23 of Algorithm 1 ('Compute centers s_1..n_empty of cells e_1..n_empty' and 'D_A.extend((s_1..n_empty, f_min))'), extending the dataset that was populated with emitter-sampled entries during Phase 1.

The discount model f_hat_A(.; psi) is regressed on the complete dataset D_A, which contains both the emitter-sampled entries collected during Phase 1 (lines 12-13) and the empty-point entries just added (lines 21-23), updating the parameters psi via the Adam-based training procedure described in Appendix C, matching line 24 of Algorithm 1 ('Regress f_hat_A on D_A').

Phase 2's dataset extension and discount model regression are executed only after Phase 1's inner loop over all W emitters (Algorithm 1 lines 7-20) has fully completed for the current iteration, so that D_A contains contributions from every emitter before empty points are added and the model is retrained, and no emitter samples solutions using a discount model updated mid-iteration.

The baseline black-box QD algorithms (CMA-MAE, DDS, MAP-Elites (line), and MAP-Elites) have been implemented correctly as described in Section 3.

MAP-Elites is implemented as described in Section 3: a grid archive that divides the measure space into axis-aligned (hyper-)rectangle cells, each storing one solution (the elite), where each iteration selects a solution from the archive, mutates it via theta' <- theta + sigma*N(0,I) (isotropic Gaussian noise), and inserts theta' into its assigned cell, replacing the current cell occupant only if it has a higher objective value.

MAP-Elites's archive tessellation T divides the measure space into a grid of axis-aligned (hyper-)rectangle cells, with each cell storing exactly one solution (the elite currently occupying that cell), per Section 3's description ('MAP-Elites produces a "grid archive" where the tessellation T divides the measure space into a grid of axis-aligned (hyper-)rectangles. Each cell in the archive stores one solution').

For every domain whose measure space exceeds 2 dimensions (10D/20D/50D LP (Sphere), 10D LP (Rastrigin), 10D LP (Flat), and all three QDDM domains), MAP-Elites uses a centroidal Voronoi tessellation (CVT) archive rather than an axis-aligned grid, per Section 3's note that grid archives require exponentially more memory in high dimensions and that prior work (Vassiliades et al., 2018) defines T as a CVT for such domains, and per Appendix C's archive configuration.

On each iteration, MAP-Elites selects one existing archive solution theta (from the currently occupied cells) to serve as the parent for mutation, per Section 3's description ('Each iteration, MAP-Elites selects an archive solution theta, mutates it to create a new solution theta'').

MAP-Elites generates the new candidate solution theta' from the selected parent theta via the isotropic Gaussian mutation operator theta' <- theta + sigma*N(0, I), where sigma is the MAP-Elites step-size hyperparameter of Table 6: sigma=0.5 for all seven benchmark domains including Arm Repertoire, and sigma=0.1 for TA (MNIST), TA (F-MNIST), and LSI (Hiker). This matches Section 3's stated mutation rule for 'a version of MAP-Elites that mutates solutions by adding isotropic Gaussian noise'.

theta' replaces the solution theta_e currently occupying cell e if and only if theta' has a strictly higher objective value than theta_e (i.e., f(theta') > f(theta_e)); if cell e is unoccupied, theta' is inserted directly, per Section 3's statement ('theta' replaces the solution in cell e if it has a higher objective value... MAP-Elites... retains elites, i.e., the best solution found in each cell').

MAP-Elites generates and evaluates lambda solutions per iteration (per the domain-specific batch size lambda in Table 6, e.g., lambda=540 for benchmark domains, lambda=180 for TA domains, lambda=36 for LSI Hiker), by repeatedly performing the select-mutate-insert cycle lambda times, matching Appendix C's statement that for MAP-Elites 'this number is equivalent to the batch size lambda'.

MAP-Elites (line) is implemented as described in Section 3: it augments MAP-Elites with the Iso+LineDD operator, generating new solutions as theta' <- theta_1 + sigma_1*N(0,I) + sigma_2*N(0,I)*(theta_2 - theta_1), where theta_1 and theta_2 are two solutions sampled from the archive, leveraging correlations between archived solutions.

On each generation step, MAP-Elites (line) samples two distinct solutions theta_1 and theta_2 from the archive to serve as parents for the Iso+LineDD mutation operator, per Section 3's formula theta' <- theta_1 + sigma_1*N(0,I) + sigma_2*N(0,I)*(theta_2 - theta_1), where 'theta_1 and theta_2 are sampled from the archive'.

MAP-Elites (line)'s Iso+LineDD operator includes an isotropic Gaussian noise term sigma_1*N(0,I) added to the base parent theta_1, matching the first noise component of the formula theta' <- theta_1 + sigma_1*N(0,I) + sigma_2*N(0,I)*(theta_2 - theta_1) from Section 3, with sigma_1 configured per Table 6 (e.g., sigma_1=0.5 for benchmark domains, sigma_1=0.1 for TA and LSI domains).

MAP-Elites (line)'s Iso+LineDD operator includes a directional line term sigma_2*N(0,I)*(theta_2 - theta_1) that leverages the correlation between the two sampled archive solutions theta_1 and theta_2, matching the second component of the formula in Section 3, with sigma_2 configured per Table 6 (sigma_2=0.2 for all domains).

MAP-Elites (line)'s new solution theta' is computed by additively combining the base parent theta_1, the isotropic noise term sigma_1*N(0,I), and the directional line term sigma_2*N(0,I)*(theta_2 - theta_1) into the single formula theta' <- theta_1 + sigma_1*N(0,I) + sigma_2*N(0,I)*(theta_2 - theta_1), exactly as stated in Section 3, rather than applying either term in isolation.

MAP-Elites (line) inserts each generated solution theta' into the archive cell corresponding to its measure values m(theta'), replacing the current cell occupant only if theta' has a higher objective value, i.e. it reuses MAP-Elites's elite-replacement rule unchanged and differs only in its mutation operator, per Section 3.

MAP-Elites (line) generates and evaluates lambda solutions per iteration using the domain-specific batch size of Table 6 (lambda=540 for the benchmark domains, 180 for the TA domains, 36 for LSI (Hiker)), matching Appendix C's statement that for the MAP-Elites algorithms the per-iteration evaluation count equals the batch size lambda.

CMA-MAE is implemented as described in Section 3, integrating CMA-ES into MAP-Elites via multiple CMA-ES emitter instances that sample solutions from N(theta*, Sigma), evaluate and insert them into the archive, compute improvement values Delta(theta) = f(theta) - f_A(m(theta)) using a discrete histogram-based discount function f_A, and use the ranking of Delta values to update each emitter's distribution parameters theta* and Sigma toward greater archive improvement.

CMA-MAE maintains one or more CMA-ES emitter instances, each sampling a batch of solutions theta_i from its Gaussian distribution N(theta*, Sigma) and evaluating each solution's objective f(theta_i) and measures m(theta_i), per Section 3 ('CMA-MAE maintains a CMA-ES instance that samples solutions theta_i from a Gaussian distribution N(theta*, Sigma). Each solution theta_i is evaluated and added to the archive').

CMA-MAE inserts each evaluated solution into its archive cell following the MAP-Elites replacement rule, replacing the cell's current occupant only if the new solution has a higher objective value, per Section 3 ('As in MAP-Elites, a new solution can only replace the cell solution theta_e if it has a higher objective value').

CMA-MAE supports multiple CMA-ES instances operating in parallel, each referred to as an emitter, with W emitters instantiated per the domain's Table 6 configuration, per Section 3 ('Multiple CMA-ES instances may operate in parallel, with each instance referred to as an emitter').

CMA-MAE represents the discount function f_A as a discrete histogram in measure space: the measure space is tessellated into cells (grid or CVT depending on domain), and each cell e stores a single scalar discount value, such that any two solutions whose measures fall in the same cell receive an identical discount value regardless of how different their measures actually are, per Section 3 ('CMA-MAE represents f_A as a histogram by tessellating the measure space into cells and storing a scalar value in each cell').

For each solution theta_i sampled by a CMA-MAE emitter, the archive improvement value is computed as Delta(theta_i) = f(theta_i) - f_A(m(theta_i)), where f_A(m(theta_i)) is the scalar discount value of the histogram cell that theta_i's measures fall into, matching the improvement definition given in Section 3 directly following the discount function description.

The ranking of the computed Delta_i values across a CMA-ES emitter's sampled batch is used to update that emitter's CMA-ES distribution parameters theta* (mean) and Sigma (covariance) in the direction of greatest archive improvement, following standard CMA-ES rank-based update rules, per Section 3 ('The ranking of the improvement values enables the CMA-ES instance to update the distribution parameters theta* and Sigma in the direction of greatest archive improvement').

Each cell's threshold value t_e is initialized to the minimum objective value f_min (rather than to the objective of a solution, as in CMA-ME), per Section 3 ('t_e is initialized to a minimum value f_min').

When a new solution theta' is inserted into cell e (i.e., it improves the objective over the current occupant), the cell's threshold t_e is updated as t_e <- (1 - alpha)*t_e + alpha*f(theta'), where alpha is the archive learning rate (0 <= alpha <= 1), reproducing the exact threshold update rule given in Section 3.

When the archive learning rate alpha = 1.0, the CMA-MAE implementation sets each cell's threshold t_e directly to the objective value of each new solution entering the cell, making CMA-MAE equivalent to CMA-ME and maximally exploration-focused, per Section 3 ('when alpha = 1.0, CMA-MAE focuses on exploration and is equivalent to CMA-ME').

When the archive learning rate alpha = 0.0, each cell's threshold t_e remains constant at f_min, so the improvement reduces to Delta(theta) = f(theta) - C and CMA-MAE performs pure single-objective optimization, per Section 3 ('When alpha = 0.0, CMA-MAE performs single-objective optimization because t_e will be constant').

Density Descent Search (DDS) is implemented as described in Section 3: it removes the discount function from CMA-MAE and instead introduces a kernel density estimator (KDE) that models the density of previously discovered solutions in measure space, ranking sampled solutions by the KDE's density estimates (prioritizing solutions in low-density regions) rather than by archive improvement, making DDS a diversity-only optimization algorithm that does not consider the objective when ranking.

DDS implements a kernel density estimator (KDE) that models the density of previously discovered solutions in measure space, replacing CMA-MAE's discrete discount-function histogram entirely, per Section 3's description that DDS 'removes the discount function from CMA-MAE and introduces a kernel density estimator (KDE) that models the density of previously discovered solutions in measure space'.

The DDS KDE is fit on a maintained buffer holding the measures of previously discovered solutions, and that buffer is updated and the density model refit as new solutions are discovered during search, so the density estimate tracks where the algorithm has already been, per Section 3's description of DDS.

DDS ranks each iteration's sampled solutions by the KDE's estimated density at their measure values, prioritizing solutions in areas of low density, entirely replacing CMA-MAE's archive-improvement-based ranking mechanism (Delta) with this density-based ranking, per Section 3's statement that 'DDS ranks solutions by the KDE's density estimates, prioritizing solutions in areas of low density'.

The DDS ranking procedure does not incorporate the objective function f(theta) at any point, confirming that DDS is a diversity-only optimization algorithm that 'does not optimize the objective, making it a diversity optimization algorithm, i.e., it only searches for solutions with diverse measures', per Section 3.

DDS still uses CMA-ES-based emitters (as in CMA-MAE) to sample and search for solutions, but the emitters' distribution parameters are updated based on the KDE density ranking instead of archive improvement ranking, consistent with DDS being built by modifying CMA-MAE's improvement mechanism while retaining its CMA-ES emitter structure, per Section 3.

DDS uses the 'No Imp.' restart rule, i.e., an emitter restarts when it no longer discovers solutions that improve the archive (in the DDS case, are added under the density-ranking criterion), as specified for all applicable domains in Table 6 ('Restart rule: No Imp.').
DDS uses the 'Filter' selection rule, as specified for all applicable domains in Table 6 ('Selection rule: Filter'), distinct from the 'mu' selection rule used by DMS and CMA-MAE.

DDS is not run in any of the three QDDM domains (TA MNIST, TA F-MNIST, LSI Hiker) because the KDE's runtime grows linearly with measure space dimensionality, making it computationally intractable in the high-dimensional QDDM measure spaces, per Section 7.1's statement 'We could not run DDS in the QDDM domains due to the KDE's runtime, which grows linearly with measure space dimensionality' and Table 6's corresponding blank ('—') entries for DDS in TA (MNIST), TA (F-MNIST), and LSI (Hiker).

The Linear Projection (LP) measure function m(theta) is implemented to partition the n-dimensional solution vector theta into k contiguous, non-overlapping blocks of size r=n/k (one-indexed), matching Appendix E.1's definition of m(theta) over blocks {jr+1, ..., (j+1)r} for j in {0,...,k-1}.

The clip(theta_i) function used inside the LP measure function is implemented exactly as defined in Appendix E.1: clip(theta_i) = theta_i if |theta_i| <= 5.12, otherwise clip(theta_i) = 5.12/theta_i, applied element-wise before summing each block.

After applying clip(.) element-wise to each block of size r, the LP measure function sums the clipped values within each block to produce a single scalar measure value per block, yielding a k-dimensional measure vector m(theta), matching Appendix E.1's equation for m(theta).

The LP measure space bounds are enforced as [-5.12r, 5.12r]^k, which follows from clip(.) bounding each theta_i to [-5.12, 5.12] and each measure being the sum of r clipped components, giving the concrete per-domain archive ranges [-256, 256]^2 for the k=2 domains (r=50), [-51.2, 51.2]^10 for the k=10 domains (r=10), [-25.6, 25.6]^20 for 20D LP (Sphere) (r=5), and [-10.24, 10.24]^50 for 50D LP (Sphere) (r=2); the [-256, 256] axis ranges of the 2D LP heatmaps in Figure 7 confirm the k=2 case.
The Sphere objective f_Sphere(theta) = sum_{i=1}^{n} theta_i^2 is implemented exactly as defined in Appendix E.1, used as one of the two base objectives for LP domain instantiations.

The Rastrigin objective f_Rastrigin(theta) = 10n + sum_{i=1}^{n} [theta_i^2 - 10*cos(2*pi*theta_i^2)] is implemented exactly as defined in Appendix E.1, used as the second base objective for LP domain instantiations. NOTE: the paper's displayed equation uses cos(2*pi*theta_i^2) rather than the standard Rastrigin cos(2*pi*theta_i) term; the implementation must match the paper's stated formula exactly as written, even if this differs from the canonical Rastrigin function.

The Flat objective f_Flat(theta) = 1 (a constant) is implemented exactly as defined in Appendix E.1, turning the domain into a pure diversity optimization domain where all solutions share the same objective value.

The Sphere and Rastrigin objectives, which require minimization by default, are converted for maximization by taking their negative values, per Appendix E.1's statement 'we convert them for maximization by taking their negative values'.

The Arm Repertoire domain (Cully & Demiris, 2017; Vassiliades & Mouret, 2018) has been implemented exactly as specified in Appendix E.2 and Section 6.1, as an inverse-kinematics domain over a planar robotic arm.

Each Arm Repertoire solution theta is an n-dimensional vector of joint angles for a planar robotic arm with n joints, per Appendix E.2 ('Arm Repertoire considers solutions theta in R^n that represent the n joint angles of a planar robotic arm with n joints').
The planar arm has n links, each of length 1, per Appendix E.2 ('a planar robotic arm with n joints and n links of length 1').

The Arm Repertoire measure function m(theta) uses forward kinematics to compute the (x, y) position of the arm's end effector from the joint angles, per Appendix E.2 ('The measure function, m(theta), uses forward kinematics to compute the (x, y) position of the end effector').
The Arm Repertoire measure space is two-dimensional, consisting of the end effector's (x, y) position, per Appendix E.2 ('thus, the measure space is two-dimensional').

The Arm Repertoire objective is f(theta) = -var(theta), the negated variance of the n joint angles, so that maximizing the objective minimizes joint-angle variance, per Appendix E.2's equation and Section 6.1 ('The objective indicates the variance of the n joint angles').

The Arm Repertoire objective has 1 added to it so that its maximum value is 1, per Appendix E.2 ('We also add 1 to the objective to normalize it to a maximum value of 1'), giving f(theta) = 1 - var(theta).
The Arm Repertoire experiments use solution dimensionality n = 100 (a 100-joint arm), per Appendix E.2 ('Our experiments consider n = 100').

Arm Repertoire uses a 10,000-cell archive arranged as a 100x100 grid over the 2D end-effector measure space, per Appendix C's archive configuration for 2D benchmark domains, with measure bounds spanning [-100, 100] in each dimension (the reachable envelope of 100 unit-length links, as confirmed by the axis ranges of the Arm Repertoire heatmaps in Figure 7).

The QDDM setting and its two new image-based domains, Triangle Arrangement (TA MNIST and F-MNIST) and Latent Space Illumination LSI (Hiker), have been implemented correctly with CVT archives from datasets, distance functions, and objectives.

The QDDM setting is implemented as specified in Section 6.2: instead of the user hand-designing a measure function, the user supplies a dataset of high-dimensional data points (images here) whose space is taken directly as the measure space S, and the archive is built so that it partitions only the region of measure space that the dataset occupies rather than the whole space, following the manifold hypothesis (Fefferman et al., 2016) invoked in Section 6.2.

The Triangle Arrangement QDDM domains, TA (MNIST) and TA (F-MNIST), have been implemented as described in Section 6.2 and Appendix E.3: 30 parameterized triangles rendered into a grayscale raster image that serves as the solution's measures, with dataset images as CVT centroids and a negative-MSE objective.

Each triangle in the Triangle Arrangement (TA) domain is parameterized by the 8-tuple (x0, y0, x1, y1, x2, y2, brightness, a), where (x0,y0), (x1,y1), (x2,y2) are the triangle's vertices and brightness/a (alpha/transparency) control its shading, matching the equation given in Appendix E.3.
A single TA solution vector theta consists of the parameters for 30 triangles concatenated together, giving each solution 30*8 = 240 parameters, per Appendix E.3.

The 30 triangles encoded in a TA solution are rendered in the order specified in the solution vector, such that later triangles are drawn on top of and occlude earlier triangles at any intersecting pixels, per Appendix E.3 ('the last triangle would end up on top of the first triangle if they intersect').

The TA domain's triangle rasterization is implemented by adapting the JAX-based implementation from EvoJAX (Tang et al., 2022; EvoJAX, 2022), rendering each solution's 30 triangles into a raster image, per Appendix E.3's statement 'we adapt the JAX (Bradbury et al., 2018) implementation from EvoJAX'.

TA images are rendered as grayscale images with all triangles drawn on a black background, per Appendix E.3 ('We consider grayscale images in our work, with the triangles all drawn on a black background').

The TA measure space is defined as the space of 28x28 grayscale images, making it 784-dimensional, per Appendix E.3 ('We define the measure space as the space of 28 x 28 grayscale images, making it 784-dimensional').

Each of the 784 TA measure dimensions is bounded to [0, 1], the range of possible brightness values of a grayscale pixel, per Appendix E.3 ('Each dimension has bounds [0, 1], i.e., the possible brightness values of a grayscale pixel').

For each TA solution theta, the measures are computed by rendering a 28x28 raster image of its 30 triangles, i.e. the measure function m(theta) is exactly the rendered pixel-value vector, per Appendix E.3 ('For each solution theta, we compute the measures by rendering a 28x28 raster image of its triangles').
For TA (MNIST), 1000 images are sampled from the MNIST dataset (Lecun et al., 1998) to serve as the desired measures for the domain, per Appendix E.3.
For TA (F-MNIST), 1000 images are sampled from the Fashion MNIST dataset (Xiao et al., 2017) to serve as the desired measures for the domain, per Appendix E.3.

The 1000 sampled images (from MNIST or Fashion MNIST, depending on the TA variant) form the centroids of the CVT archive directly, rather than centroids computed by k-means clustering, per Appendix E.3 ('These 1000 images form the centroids of the CVT archive').

To determine the closest CVT centroid when inserting a TA solution into the archive, the Euclidean distance is computed between the solution's measures (its rendered 28x28 image, flattened to 784 dimensions) and each of the 1000 centroid images, per Appendix E.3 ('we compute the Euclidean distance between the solution's measures... and each centroid').

For each TA solution, the objective is defined as the negative mean squared error (MSE) between the solution's measures (rendered image) and the centroid image of the closest CVT cell, per Appendix E.3 ('the objective is the negative mean squared error between the solution's measures and the centroid to which it is closest').

The TA objective (negative MSE) is normalized to the range [0, 1] by adding 1 to it, per Appendix E.3 ('To normalize this objective to a range of [0, 1], we add 1 to it'), so that solutions closely resembling their assigned centroid image receive objective values near 1.

The TA objective design (negative MSE against the closest MNIST/F-MNIST centroid) enables solutions that resemble a real MNIST or Fashion MNIST image to replace solutions that do not resemble such images in the archive, consistent with Appendix E.3's stated purpose ('This objective enables solutions that resemble an MNIST image to replace solutions that do not').

The Latent Space Illumination domain LSI (Hiker) has been implemented as described in Section 6.2 and Appendix E.4: StyleGAN3 latent vectors as solutions, generated face images as measures, a 10,000-cell CVT archive whose centroids are LHQ256 landscape images, CLIP-score cell assignment, and the three-term objective.

Each LSI (Hiker) solution theta is a 512-dimensional latent vector in the w-space of StyleGAN3 (not the w+-space, which assigns a distinct style vector per layer and is much higher-dimensional, e.g. 8,192- or 7,168-dimensional), per Appendix E.4.
The LSI (Hiker) domain uses the pretrained StyleGAN3 (Karras et al., 2021a) checkpoint stylegan3-t-ffhqu-256x256.pkl to generate 256x256 RGB face images from latent vectors, per Appendix E.4.

The LSI (Hiker) measure space is defined as the space of 256x256x3 RGB images, and the measure function m(theta) outputs the face image generated by passing the solution theta through StyleGAN3, per Appendix E.4.
10,000 landscape images are sampled from the LHQ256 dataset (Skorokhodov et al., 2021) to specify the desired measures for the LSI (Hiker) domain, per Appendix E.4.

The 10,000 sampled LHQ256 landscape images form the centroids of the CVT archive directly (not centroids computed via k-means or other clustering), consistent with the QDDM approach of using dataset points as CVT centroids, per Appendix E.4 ('These images form the centroids of a CVT archive').

When inserting an LSI (Hiker) solution into the archive, the closest CVT centroid is determined by computing the CLIP score (Radford et al., 2021), specifically using the ViT-B/32 model of CLIP, between the generated face image and each landscape centroid image, per Appendix E.4 ('we compute the closest centroid with CLIP score... specifically with the ViT-B/32 model of CLIP').

The CLIP-score-based cell assignment in LSI (Hiker) is designed so that a hiker's appearance is associated with the centroid/landscape that is semantically closest to them (e.g., a hiker in a thick jacket assigned to a cold mountain landscape, a hiker in thin clothes assigned to a beach landscape), consistent with the qualitative example and Figure 2 described in Appendix E.4 and Section 1.
The LSI (Hiker) objective includes the term f_prompt, computed as the CLIP score between the generated face image and the text prompt 'A photo of the face of a hiker.', per Appendix E.4.

The LSI (Hiker) objective includes the term f_centroid, computed as the CLIP score between the generated face image and the landscape centroid image to which the solution is assigned in the CVT archive, per Appendix E.4, resulting in images that more closely match the landscape specified by the assigned centroid.

The LSI (Hiker) regularizer is parameterized by first sampling 10,000 points in StyleGAN3's w-space and computing their mean and standard deviation, which together define the reference training distribution, per Appendix E.4 ('We sample 10,000 points in w-space and compute their mean and standard deviation').

The LSI (Hiker) objective applies an L2 penalty f_reg to any latent vector theta that strays too far outside the w-space distribution characterized by that mean and standard deviation, following the regularizer loss of Fontaine & Nikolaidis (2023), per Appendix E.4 and Section 6.2.

The final LSI (Hiker) objective is computed exactly as f = (f_prompt + f_centroid)/2 - f_reg, matching the equation given in Appendix E.4, such that the objective stays between 0 and 1 if the algorithm remains within StyleGAN3's training distribution, but can become negative if f_reg incurs a high regularization penalty.

For LSI (Hiker), CLIP embeddings for all 10,000 archive centroid landscape images are precomputed once, and nearest-neighbor cell assignment for new solutions is performed by embedding the new solution's generated image with CLIP and then searching over the precomputed 512-dimensional centroid embeddings (via scikit-learn's NearestNeighbors), rather than repeatedly recomputing CLIP scores against raw images, per Appendix C.2.

The two dependent variables used to evaluate every algorithm in every domain, QD Score and Coverage, are implemented exactly as defined in Section 7.

QD Score is computed as the sum of the objective values of all solutions currently stored in the archive, mirroring the relaxed QD objective of Section 2, per Section 7 ('QD Score (Pugh et al., 2016) represents overall performance by summing the objectives of all solutions in the archive').

Coverage is computed as the percentage of archive cells that contain a solution, per Section 7 ('Coverage indicates how much of the measure space has been explored by computing the percentage of archive cells that have a solution in them').

The objective in every domain is normalized so that its maximum attainable value is 1, per Section 7 ('Note that the objective is normalized to have a maximum value of 1 in all domains'), which is what makes QD Score comparable across domains.

Because the objective is capped at 1 and QD Score sums over occupied archive cells, the logged QD Score never exceeds the archive's cell count (10,000 for the benchmark and LSI (Hiker) archives, 1,000 for the TA archives), and in the LP (Flat) domains, where every objective is exactly 1.0, the logged QD Score equals the number of occupied cells exactly.
The statistical analysis pipeline described in Section 7.1 has been implemented, comprising the normality check, the homoscedasticity test, the omnibus test, and the post-hoc pairwise test.

Each domain is analysed as a between-groups study in which the algorithm is the independent variable and QD Score and Coverage are the two dependent variables, per Section 7 ('In each domain, we conduct a between-groups study with the algorithm as the independent variable... We consider two dependent variables').
The per-domain, per-metric result distributions are checked for normality by visual inspection, per Section 7.1 ('Visual inspection showed the results were normally distributed').
Levene's test is applied to each domain/metric setting to test the homogeneity-of-variance assumption, per Section 7.1 ('Levene's test showed most settings were non-homoscedastic').

A Welch's one-way ANOVA is conducted separately in each domain for each dependent variable, chosen over the standard one-way ANOVA specifically because Levene's test indicated non-homoscedasticity, per Section 7.1 ('Thus, to analyze the results, we conducted Welch's one-way ANOVA in each domain for each dependent variable').

Games-Howell pairwise post-hoc comparisons are performed between every pair of algorithms whenever the corresponding ANOVA is significant, per Section 7.1 ('All ANOVAs were significant (p < 0.001...), so we performed pairwise comparisons with the Games-Howell test').

The reproduced Levene's tests indicate that most domain/metric settings are non-homoscedastic even though the results are visually normally distributed, reproducing the assumption-check outcome that motivates the Welch/Games-Howell choice in Section 7.1.

The reproduced ablation results show that the difference between restart rules is particularly prominent in 10D LP (Flat), where the 'basic' restart rule achieves a mean QD Score of only 2,064.10 while the restart rule of 100 achieves a mean QD Score of 7,982.15, consistent with Appendix D.3's statement ('The difference is particularly prominent in 10D LP (Flat), where the "basic" restart rule receives a mean QD Score of 2,064.10 while the restart rule of 100 receives a mean QD Score of 7,982.15').

The observed benefit of the fixed restart rule (100) in higher-dimensional (10D) measure spaces is analyzed as resulting from the emitter potentially 'hacking' the discount model by generating solutions in successive nearby low-discount-value regions without genuinely improving archive coverage, an effect that is more prevalent in high-dimensional measure spaces because there are exponentially more 'nearby areas' with low discount values, and that a fixed restart schedule forces the emitter to restart before it can converge to exploit this behavior, consistent with the explanation in Appendix D.3.
